facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Chand Baori is an architectural wonder with 3,500 perfectly symmetrical, narrow steps.
facts.text: Chand Baori contains approximately 3,500 narrow, symmetrical stone steps arranged in double flights across three terraced sides of the well.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The phenomenal structure is 19.5 meters in depth and features 1000 narrow steps, spanning 13 storeys.
facts.text: The stepwell structure descends across 13 storeys into the earth to reach the deep regional water table.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The phenomenal structure is 19.5 meters in depth and features 1000 narrow steps, spanning 13 storeys.
facts.text: The total subterranean depth of Chand Baori measures approximately 19.5 metres below the surface level.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: However, no epigraphic evidence has been found regarding the construction of the Chand Baori or the adjoining Harshat Mata Temple. Based on similarities in style and carvings with the terraced temples of Paranagar and Mandore, the Baori can be dated to the 8th-9th century.
facts.source_name: Morna Livingston / Steps to Water: The Ancient Stepwells of India
facts.text: Historians date the core stepped structure to the 8th to 9th century CE based on architectural comparisons, though no primary foundation inscriptions survive at the site.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: According to Morna Livingston in Steps to Water: The Ancient Stepwells of India, Chand Baori is one of the few stepwells that has 'two classical periods of water building in a single setting'. The oldest parts of the step-well date from the 8th century onwards. An upper palace building was added to the site, which can be seen from the tabulated arches used by the Chauhan rulers.
facts.source_name: Morna Livingston / Steps to Water: The Ancient Stepwells of India
facts.text: Architectural studies reveal that the stepwell incorporates two classical eras, with the 8th-century lower stone steps overlaid in the 18th century by arcaded Mughal-style galleries and pavilions.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: One of the largest stepwells in the world, Chand Baori was built to conserve water and provide a respite from the intense heat.
facts.text: Due to subterranean depth, steep masonry shading, and continuous evaporative cooling from the pool below, ambient air at the bottom of the well remains 5 to 6 degrees Celsius cooler than at ground surface.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Local people of Abhaneri tales have it that this massive stepwell, imagine a structure with 3500 steps and 13 stories, was built in just one night by ghosts.
facts.text: Local oral folklore claims that spirits or ghosts built the entire 13-storey stepwell in a single night under royal orders.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: It is claimed about these stairs that once someone gets down from a stair, they cannot come back from that stair.
facts.text: According to local legend, the maze-like geometry was designed so that no visitor could ever step on the same flight of stairs twice while ascending.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: There is a cave named Andheri-Ujali inside the stepwell. From this cave a 17 km long tunnel originates in the village of Bhandarej.
facts.text: A popular regional legend asserts that an subterranean tunnel inside the baori's Andheri-Ujali passage stretches 17 kilometres to the historic settlement of Bhandarej.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: The classical Indian texts on architecture (Vastu) like Aparajitapriccha or Vishvakarma's Vastushastra call this design a vijay vapi.
facts.text: Classical Indian architectural texts, including the Aparajitapriccha and Vastushastra, classify the inverted stepped-pyramid cistern plan exemplified by Chand Baori as a 'vijaya vapi'.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Excavated stones of the temple are now kept by the Archaeological Survey of India in the arcades of the well.
facts.text: Excavated architectural stone fragments and sculptures recovered by archaeologists around the site originate from the adjoining 8th-century Harshat Mata temple complex.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: This is a photo of ASI monument number N-RJ-74... Construction of Boundary wall in the area made encroachment free at Chand Baori, Abhaneri, Dist. Dausa.
facts.text: Chand Baori is catalogued and protected as a centrally preserved monument of national importance under Archaeological Survey of India inventory number N-RJ-74.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The temple's original builder is unknown, but historians theorize that it may have been built by a Gurjara-Pratihara king, possibly in association with a local Chahamana vassal.
facts.source_name: Michael W. Meister / Archaeological Survey of India
facts.text: Scholars debate the patron of the site, with one faction attributing its foundation to King Chanda of the Nikumbha dynasty and another linking its artistic style to the imperial Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Mihira Bhoja.
